catalog_quote: II.4. Tone and morphology. Like most of Niger-Congo languages (Clements 2000: 152; Creissels 1994: 177), Koalib is a tone language, i.e. the tonal melody associated to each syllable of a word has a distinctive value. Koalib has two tone levels: - high, signaled by an acute accent (°): ... saliva. - low, signaled by a grave accent ...: ... eggs. These two levels can combine to form several types of modulations, the most common of which is the falling tone (begins high and ends low), signaled by a circumflex accent: ... water. Although it is possible to provide several tens of lexical pairs of the ... type, the highest functional load of tone obtains in morphology

sweep_summary: Koalib-Rere (koal1240, Heibanic) is not in the catalog. The one works with stress in the title, Chai, Kunda, Rodríguez & Rose 2022 'Prosody of declaratives and questions in Rere (Koalib)' (OUP, DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198869740.003.0011), is a sentence-intonation study of a tone language (boundary tones L%/H%, H lowering, upsweep, clitic tones per the Crossref abstract and Google Books snippets pp. 298-331); it is paywalled (OUP 403, Unpaywall closed, no author PDF), and nothing reachable from it mentions word stress. Extra open sources downloaded and read with): Quint 2006 'Do you speak Kordofanian?' (§II.4: 'Koalib is a tone language.. two tone levels' plus falling tone), Quint 2024 imperatives (§2.1: two phonological tones H/L, contour F=HL, citing Quint 2006: 145-165; 2009: 129-148), Quint & Koko 2025, Quint 2022 (acute in Koalib marks tone, whereas in non-tonal Nyun it marks 'accent tonique'), Boychev 2013 MA thesis, and the open-access Demir Nalci, Kunda & Rose 2025 SAL paper (§2.1: 'Rere has two level tones, H, L, and a falling HL'). None contains any statement on word stress or accent placement. No best new stress statement found. Highest-priority unread source: Quint (& Kokko) 2009 The Phonology of Koalib, Rüdiger Köppe (chapters on vowels, consonants, tonal system, syllable structure, orthography; HAL record halshs-00584041 without file; publisher PDF for sale; Harvard print Widener Library PL8393.95.N57 Q5613 2009), plus its 2006 French original (L'Harmattan; Harvard print PL8393). chapter cannot be excluded (medium priority).

new_statements.quote: III. Tonology. Koalib is a tone language, as are most Niger-Congo languages (Creissels 1994: 177). There are two kinds of tones in Koalib: register tones distinguished by height (high, low and, potentially, mid); and modulated contour tones (falling, rising). Tones are marked by diacritics placed over the vowel of the syllable concerned.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Koalib (Rere) is described as a tone language with two register tones (H, L; a phonetic mid) and contour tones (falling, rising); the dedicated phonology says nothing about word stress at all — Google's full-text index of the book has no token 'stress', 'stressed', 'prominence', 'accentual' or 'prosodic', while control words (vowel, syllable, tone, pitch, loudness, tonic) hit. No source locates a stress position.
new_statements.exceptions: Older group-level remark, Stevenson 1957 (Afrika und Übersee 41), Koalib-Moro (= Heiban) group phonetic summary, item 2 (reconstructed from overlapping Google Books snippets, saved as gs_9/gs_10/gs_2/gs_31/): 'Dynamic accent (stress), accompanied by high or low tone, plays a greater role than syllable pitch, but is not equally prominent in all members of the group. In most languages a few lexical tone doublets are to be found, e.g. LARO: 'yore axes 'yorè fences OTORO: 'gwùtù buttock gwutú many.' This asserts stress exists group-wide but gives no position and no Koalib-specific data; it is superseded by Quint 2009 and Chai et al. 2022, which analyse the system purely as tone plus boundary tones.
new_statements.domain_note: Quint 2009 describes the Rere dialect (Abri area) at word level (lexical and morphological tone). Chai et al. 2022 and Demir Nalci et al. 2025 (Rere, UCSD group) treat sentence prosody and tonal case marking with no stress dimension. Stevenson's remark is about the whole Koalib-Moro group, from 1950s survey fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern sources describe the Rere dialect (Quint: Abri area; UCSD group: 'Rere (Koalib)'), Glottolog dialect ngir1247 (Ngirere) under koal1240; Quint notes 'Koalib' is an Arabic exonym. The only explicit stress remark (Stevenson 1957) is for the whole Koalib-Moro = Heiban group (Glottolog heib1242), not Koalib specifically.

tone_statements.quote: Rere has three lexical tones: high H, low L, and falling HL as illustrated by these minimal pairs (Quint 2009:129). [...] Due to these contrasts, one must conclude that HL is a distinct tone from H and L, even if its distribution within nominal and verbal stems favors heavy syllables. See Quint (2009) for further discussion of tone distribution. Tone is also used to express grammatical distinctions in verbs. Aspectual categories are differentiated by affixes as well as by tone patterns. For example, the recent perfect and remote perfect both have a prefix m-, but have different tone patterns. Remote perfect is all low-toned, while recent perfect has a low-toned prefix and lexical tone on the stem, either LH, HH or HL.

tone_statements.n_tones: 3 (H, L, falling HL); boundary tones L%, H%

tone_statements.citation: Chai, Yuan. 2020. The role of tone in TAM, verb class, and subject agreement in Rere. Abstract accepted for the 51st Annual Conference on African Linguistics (ACAL 51; scheduled May 2020, conference cancelled due to COVID-19). 1 p. Author's website (PDF created 2019-12-13; no author name printed on the page, authorship from the author's publications list and file metadata 'abstract_5thdraft_ACAL_YC').
tone_statements.quote: Resembling other Kordofanian languages (Moro: Rose, 2013; Lumun: Smits, 2017), Rere uses tone to mark TAM, subject, and verb class. The tone on verb stem reflects the interaction among grammatical tone (TAM), lexical tone (verb class), and phonological tone spreading (subject). [...] There are two classes for TAM melody: non-replacive class where the lexical tone of the verb is preserved, and replacive class where all the TBUs in the verb are overwritten into L tone. [...] The subject prefixes initiate an unbounded right-ward H spreading up to another H tone (3b), which overwrites the L tone of TAM and lexical class.
tone_statements.locator: single-page abstract, paragraphs 1-2 and 'Subject agreement' paragraph
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 levels (H, L) in verb melodies; lexical verb classes LH, HL, HH

readall_conflicts: One disagreement of prosodic type, none of placement. The catalog (Quint 2006 Bergen paper; Quint 2009 The Phonology of Koalib; Quint 2020 Oxford Handbook) treats Koalib as a tone language (H/L registers plus contour tones, lexical and morphological tone contrasts) and no source held by the project states a stress position. Tucker & Bryan 1966 ch. 18a, seen here only in snippets, relays Stevenson's 1956-57 group-level view that in the Koalib-Moro (Heiban) languages 'dynamic Stress, accompanied by High or Low tone, plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such, but is not equally prominent in all languages', with tone 'not yet fully investigated' and examples unmarked. That is a historical, second-hand, hedged dissent on whether stress or tone dominates; it gives no stress placement, says nothing about Koalib individually, and does not outweigh Quint's first-hand phonology, so the catalog's tonal coding stands and nothing new is codable from this work.

sources.quote: Koalib has two phonological tones (Quint 2006: 145–165; 2009: 129–148), namely high (H, see (1)), and low (L, see (2)). It also has several contour tones, the most frequent being a falling tone (F, see (3)), which can ultimately be analyzed as a succession of a high and a low tone, i.e., F=HL. [Quint 2024] — En koalib, les accents représentent les tons (haut (aigu) [á], bas (grave) [à], modulé descendant ... [Quint 2022: 'In Koalib the accent marks represent tones (high (acute), low (grave), falling ...)']
sources.locator: Quint 2024 §2.1 (p. 2); Quint 2022 fn. on transcription (p. 4 of PDF, line 210 of text dump); Boychev 2013 §1 pp. 4-5
sources.note: All four are morphosyntactic works whose phonological preliminaries describe only the H/L(+HL) tone system and vowel harmony; the only occurrences of 'stress' (Quint 2024, 2 hits) are the ordinary verb 'to stress a point'. Quint 2022 contrasts Koalib (acute = high tone) with Nyun, 'langue non tonale', where the acute marks 'la place de l'accent tonique' — a stress statement for Nyun, not for Koalib. Silent on Koalib word stress.

sources.citation: Chai, Yuan. 2020. The role of tone in TAM, verb class, and subject agreement in Rere. Abstract accepted for the 51st Annual Conference on African Linguistics (ACAL 51; scheduled May 2020, conference cancelled due to COVID-19). 1 p. Author's website (PDF created 2019-12-13; no author name printed on the page, authorship from the author's publications list and file metadata 'abstract_5thdraft_ACAL_YC').
sources.quote: Resembling other Kordofanian languages (Moro: Rose, 2013; Lumun: Smits, 2017), Rere uses tone to mark TAM, subject, and verb class. The tone on verb stem reflects the interaction among grammatical tone (TAM), lexical tone (verb class), and phonological tone spreading (subject). [...] There are two classes for TAM melody: non-replacive class where the lexical tone of the verb is preserved, and replacive class where all the TBUs in the verb are overwritten into L tone. [...] The subject prefixes initiate an unbounded right-ward H spreading up to another H tone (3b), which overwrites the L tone of TAM and lexical class.
sources.locator: single-page abstract, paragraphs 1-2 and 'Subject agreement' paragraph
sources.note: First-hand analysis of verb tone: tone marks TAM, subject and verb class; three lexical verb tone classes (LH, HL, HH); non-replacive TAMs (future with H-toned prefix kw-, recent past and habitual with L-toned kw-) keep lexical stem tone, replacive TAMs (perfective, progressive, remote past) overwrite the verb with L; habitual prefix H spreads rightward neutralising LH and HH; 1SG/2SG subject prefixes trigger unbounded rightward H spreading up to the next H.

sources.quote: The prosodic system of declarative sentences and questions in Rere (Koalib), a Niger-Congo language of Sudan, is characterized by pitch raising and lowering, which target boundary positions and particular tones. Declarative utterances are marked by a final L% boundary tone. [...] Polar questions are marked by a final low-toned clitic. [...] Finally, a high tone added at the left edge of the verb marks wh-ex-situ questions as well as similar constructions.
sources.locator: Crossref abstract; Google Books search-within snippets pp. 298, 303, 309, 315, 323, 329, 331
sources.note: Modern instrumental prosody study of Rere with a background section on the tonal system; the most likely modern place for an explicit remark on the absence (or presence) of word-level stress/prominence.

tone.quote: Rere has three lexical tones: high H, low L, and falling HL as illustrated by these minimal pairs (Quint 2009:129). [...] Due to these contrasts, one must conclude that HL is a distinct tone from H and L, even if its distribution within nominal and verbal stems favors heavy syllables. See Quint (2009) for further discussion of tone distribution. Tone is also used to express grammatical distinctions in verbs. Aspectual categories are differentiated by affixes as well as by tone patterns. For example, the recent perfect and remote perfect both have a prefix m-, but have different tone patterns. Remote perfect is all low-toned, while recent perfect has a low-toned prefix and lexical tone on the stem, either LH, HH or HL.
tone.locator: Section 2 'Lexical and grammatical tones', author-manuscript pp. 2-3; published chapter pp. 298-333, page of this passage not established
tone.n_tones: 3 (H, L, falling HL); boundary tones L%, H%
tone.says: Section 2: Rere has three lexical tones, H, L and falling HL (HL restricted to final heavy syllables in noun roots but contrastive on short affix vowels, hence a distinct toneme); extensive grammatical tone: aspect distinguished by tone patterns (remote perfect all-L vs recent perfect L prefix + lexical stem tone LH/HH/HL), subject/object person marking by tone, case marked by tone on nouns.
